div.head: IV Eg 2.2
div.ab: Sy þeahhwæðere þes ræd gemæne eallum leodscipe, ægðer ge Anglum ge Denum ge Bryttum, on ælcum ende mines anwealdes, to ðy þæt earm ⁊ eadig mote ágan þæt hy mid rihte gestrynað, ⁊ þeof nyte, hwær he þyfþe befæste, þeah he hwæt stele, ⁊ him swa geborgen sy heora unwilles, þæt heora to fela ne losigen.

Sy þeahhwæðere þes ræd gemæne eallum leodscype, ægðer ge Englum ge Denum ge Bryttum, on ælcum ende mines anwealdes, to ðy þæt earm ⁊ eadig mote agan þæt hi mid rihte gestrynað, ⁊ þeof nyte, hwær he þeofte befæste, ðeah he hwæt stele, ⁊ him swa geborgen sy heora unwilles, þæt heora to feola ne losien.

Sit tamen hoc nostrum consilium in commune omnibus tám Danis quam Anglis adque Bryttonibus, undique in potestatis nostre finibus, ut unicuique, siue locupleti siue [e]genti, cum pacis tranquillitate liceat possidere quod iure hereditario adquisierit ac legitime.

Sy þeahhwæðere þes ræd gemæne eallum leodscype, ægðer ge Englum ge Denum ge Bryttum, on ælcum ende mines anwealdes, to ðy þæt earm ⁊ eadig mote agan þæt hi mid rihte gestrynað, ⁊ þeof nyte hwær he þeofte befæste ðeah he hwæt stele, ⁊ him swa geborgen sy, heora unwilles, þæt heora to feola ne losien.

Nichtsdestoweniger sei folgende Verordnung gemeinschaftlich allem Volke, sowohl Engländern wie Nordleuten und Brythonen, in jedem Bezirke meines Gebiets, damit Arm und Reich, was sie rechtmässig erwerben, besitzen könne, und ein Dieb, wenn er schon etwas stiehlt, vergeblich suche, wo er Gestohlenes unterbringe, und vor ihnen [den Dieben man] gegen ihren Willen so geschützt sei, dass nicht ihrer zu viele entkommen.

Nevertheless let the following ordinance be common to all the people, English as well as Northmen and Britons, in every part of my dominion, so that poor and rich may possess what they lawfully acquire, and a thief, even if he steals something, may look in vain for where to dispose of the stolen goods, and [people] may be so protected against them [the thieves] in spite of them that not too many of them escape.

The following measure, however, shall apply generally to the whole nation—to the English, Danes and Britons in every part of my dominion—to the end that rich and poor may possess what they have lawfully acquired; and that thieves, even if they steal anything, may not know where to deposit their stolen goods; and that, little as they may like it, such precautions be taken against them that very few of them may escape.

Nevertheless, this measure is to be common to all the nation, whether Englishmen, Danes or Britons, in every province of my dominion, to the end that poor man and rich may possess what they rightly acquire, and a thief may not know where to dispose of stolen goods, although he steal anything, and against their will they be so guarded against, that few of them shall escape.

note.seg: Über die Gemeinrechtlichkeit vgl. o. 1, 6; u. 12. 14
On the law's being common to all cf. above 1, 6; below 12. 14
Vgl. Gl Briten 2. Die Kelten Südbritanniens heissen Bryttas, Brettas (samt dorther gekommenen Bretonen; Ann. Agsax. 890); Toller Dict.
Cf. Gl Briten 2. The Celts of southern Britain are called Bryttas, Brettas (including Bretons who had come from there; Ann. Agsax. 890); Toller Dict.

Die Zufügung der Versio ‘nach Erbrecht’ ist unpassend, denn 3—11 behandelt Eg nur die durch Kauf oder Tausch erworbene Fahrnis.—Hier wird einmal der Beweggrund des Gesetzes (s. d. Gl 9g. 18a) genannt. Vgl. Gl Kaufzeugen 1. 7b

The Versio's addition ‘by right of inheritance’ is inappropriate, for in 3—11 Eg deals only with movables acquired by purchase or exchange.—Here for once the motive of the law (see that word in Gl 9g. 18a) is stated. Cf. Gl Kaufzeugen 1. 7b
Den Satzschluss benutzt Versio hinter 3, 1 und wiederholt den Grundgedanken des Gesetzes, die Hinderung des Diebstahls (s. d. Gl 6, wo dies nachzutragen) u. 14
The Versio uses the end of the sentence after 3, 1 and repeats the fundamental idea of the law, the prevention of theft (see that word in Gl 6, where this is to be added), below 14
‘hinliefere, anvertraue, überantworte’; der Dorfhirt darf gestohlenes Vieh nicht übernehmen; u. 8
‘hand over, entrust, deliver up’; the village herdsman may not take over stolen cattle; below 8

Liebermann points out that Edgar is to be regarded as the first to bring the Danes definitely within the sphere of English law-making since A. and G. and E. and G. are treaties made between the Danes and Wessex and confirming the separate power of each.

The reference is perhaps to the Cornish Celts and the Welsh under his rule on the borders of Wales, cf. Birch, 1267: He (God) hæfð nu gewyld to minum anwealde Scottas ⁊ Cumbras ⁊ eac swylce Bryttas ⁊ eall þæt ðis igland him on innan hæfð. In this charter Liebermann takes Cumbras to refer to Wales (cf. modern Welsh Cymru). It may be noted that Britland is frequently used for Wales in the eleventh century.
